title: IIR Filter Design
description: Design IIR filters from analog prototypes: Butterworth and Chebyshev orders, impulse invariance and its aliasing, and the bilinear transform with prewarping.

study.title: From analog prototype to digital filter
study.body: Classic IIR design borrows decades of analog filter theory. Translate the digital specifications into analog ones, design a Butterworth, Chebyshev or elliptic $H_c(s)$ that meets them, then map $H_c(s)$ to $H(z)$. The mapping must take the $j\Omega$ axis to the unit circle and stable analog poles (left half plane) to stable digital poles (inside the circle). Two mappings dominate: **impulse invariance** and the **bilinear transform**. The parameter $T_d$ used in the mapping is a design variable; it is not necessarily the sampling period of the final system.

study.title: Butterworth filters
study.body: The Butterworth low-pass is **maximally flat**: monotonic in both bands, −3 dB at $\Omega_c$, falling at $20N$ dB/decade. With a pass-band loss of at most $A_p$ dB at $\Omega_p$ and at least $A_s$ dB at $\Omega_s$, the minimum order follows from the magnitude formula. Then choose $\Omega_c$ to meet one band edge exactly, e.g. $\Omega_c = \Omega_p/(10^{A_p/10} - 1)^{1/2N}$; the other edge is then met with margin.

study.title: Explore: Butterworth poles
study.body: $|H_c(j\Omega)|^2 = H_c(s)H_c(-s)$ at $s = j\Omega$ has $2N$ poles equally spaced on a circle of radius $\Omega_c$. The $N$ in the left half plane belong to the stable $H_c(s)$; they sit at angles $\pi(2k + N - 1)/(2N)$, $k = 1 \ldots N$, symmetric about the real axis, with one real pole when $N$ is odd. Drag $N$.

study.title: Explore: Chebyshev and elliptic filters
study.body: Spreading the error evenly gives sharper filters for the same order. **Chebyshev I**: equiripple in the pass band (here 1 dB, $\varepsilon^2 = 10^{0.1} - 1$), monotonic in the stop band. **Chebyshev II**: monotonic pass band, equiripple stop band. **Elliptic**: equiripple in both, the lowest order of all, at the price of the most nonlinear phase. Drag $N$: the Chebyshev filter (green) falls much faster just past $\Omega_p$ than the Butterworth (grey, −3 dB at $\Omega_p$).

study.title: Impulse invariance
study.body: Sample the analog impulse response: $h[n] = T_dh_c(nT_d)$. Write $H_c(s)$ in partial fractions; each pole $s_k$ becomes a digital pole $z_k = e^{s_kT_d}$, and frequencies map linearly, $\omega = \Omega T_d$. But sampling aliases: $H(e^{j\omega})$ is the sum of shifted copies of $H_c$, so the method only works for responses that are (nearly) band-limited, like low-pass and band-pass filters. It cannot make a high-pass filter.

study.title: Explore: aliasing in impulse invariance
study.body: First-order example: $H_c(s) = \Omega_c/(s + \Omega_c)$ gives $H(z) = \Omega_cT_d/(1 - e^{-\Omega_cT_d}z^{-1})$. The digital response (green) follows the analog one (dashed, plotted at $\Omega = \omega/T_d$) only while $\Omega_cT_d$ is small. Two effects grow with $\Omega_cT_d$. **Aliasing**: $|H_c|$ falls only as $1/\Omega$, so the shifted copies overlap and the response near $\omega = \pi$ never gets small. **The jump at $t = 0$**: $h_c(t)$ jumps from 0 to $\Omega_c$, and $h[0] = T_dh_c(0^+)$ takes the full value, while the sum of shifted copies corresponds to the mid-point of the jump. That adds the constant $T_dh_c(0^+)/2 = \Omega_cT_d/2$, which causes most of the excess DC gain when $\Omega_cT_d$ is small. (All-pole prototypes of order 2 or more, such as Butterworth, have a continuous $h_c(t)$ and only alias.)

study.title: Explore: the bilinear transform
study.body: The substitution below maps the whole $j\Omega$ axis onto the unit circle exactly once and the left half plane inside the circle: no aliasing, and stability is preserved. The price is a nonlinear **frequency warping**, $\Omega = \frac{2}{T_d}\tan(\omega/2)$: $\Omega = \infty$ lands at $\omega = \pi$. So **prewarp**: convert the digital band edges with this formula, design the analog filter there, then transform. $T_d$ cancels and can be chosen freely. Drag the digital frequency to see where it comes from on the analog axis.

study.title: FIR or IIR?
study.body: Example specifications: $\omega_p = 0.2\pi$, $\omega_s = 0.3\pi$, 1 dB pass-band ripple, 40 dB stop band. Bilinear designs need $N$ = 12 (Butterworth), 6 (Chebyshev I) or 4 (elliptic); an equiripple FIR filter needs $M \approx 27$. **IIR** wins on order and delay for sharp magnitude specs. **FIR** offers exactly linear phase, guaranteed stability, no limit cycles and robustness to coefficient quantization, and its symmetry halves the multiplications. With linear-phase needs (data, images, audio crossovers) choose FIR; for low cost and low delay, IIR.

steps.title: IIR design via analog filters
steps.body: Most IIR filters are designed by translating the digital specifications into analog ones, designing an analog prototype $H_c(s)$ with well-known formulas, and mapping it to $H(z)$. The mapping must keep stable filters stable and map the $j\Omega$ axis to the unit circle.

steps.title: The Butterworth prototype
steps.body: The Butterworth magnitude is flat at DC, −3 dB at $\Omega_c$ and falls at $20N$ dB per decade far above it. The loss at any frequency follows directly from the formula below.

steps.prompt: An order-{{N}} Butterworth low-pass has its −3 dB frequency at $\Omega_c$. How many dB of attenuation does it have at $\Omega$ = {{r}}$\,\Omega_c$?
An analog Butterworth low-pass may lose at most {{Ap}} dB at $\Omega_p$ and must attenuate at least {{As}} dB at $\Omega_s$ = {{r}}$\,\Omega_p$. Find the minimum order $N$.

steps.title: Chebyshev and elliptic prototypes
steps.body: Butterworth spends its accuracy near DC. Letting the error ripple evenly gives a steeper cutoff for the same order: Chebyshev I ripples in the pass band, Chebyshev II in the stop band, elliptic in both. Drag $N$ to compare a 1 dB Chebyshev I with a Butterworth.

steps.prompt: Match each analog prototype to its magnitude response.
pairs: ripple in both bands, lowest order
steps.explanation: The more freedom the error gets, the lower the order: Butterworth (no ripple) needs the highest order, elliptic (ripple in both bands) the lowest. Chebyshev I and II sit in between, with the ripple in the pass band or in the stop band.

steps.prompt: An order-{{N}} Butterworth low-pass must lose exactly {{Ap}} dB at $\Omega_p = 2\pi \cdot$ {{fp|Hz}}. Find its −3 dB frequency $\Omega_c$ in rad/s.
steps.explanation: $1 + (\Omega_p/\Omega_c)^{2N} = 10^{A_p/10}$, so $\Omega_c = \Omega_p/(10^{A_p/10} - 1)^{1/2N}$ = {{Op|rad/s}} / ({{10^(Ap/10)-1||4}})^{1/{{2*N}}} = {{Op/(10^(Ap/10) - 1)^(1/(2*N))|rad/s}}. It lies above $\Omega_p$ because the loss at $\Omega_p$ is less than 3 dB.

steps.prompt: For the same pass-band and stop-band specifications, a Chebyshev I filter never needs a higher order than a Butterworth filter.
steps.explanation: The Chebyshev I magnitude uses the whole allowed pass-band ripple, and among all polynomial ('all-pole') filters with that ripple it falls fastest beyond $\Omega_p$. So it meets the stop-band requirement at the same or a lower order; often about half the Butterworth order for sharp specifications.

lessons.title: Impulse invariance and the bilinear transform

steps.title: Impulse invariance
steps.body: Sample the analog impulse response, $h[n] = T_dh_c(nT_d)$. Each analog pole $s_k$ becomes a digital pole $e^{s_kT_d}$, and frequencies map linearly, $\omega = \Omega T_d$. Sampling a response that is not band-limited aliases.

steps.prompt: Impulse invariance with $T_d = 1/f_s$, $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}, maps the analog pole pair $s = -{{sg}} \pm j2\pi \cdot$ {{fd|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the digital poles.
ask.explanation: $z = e^{sT_d} = e^{-\sigma T_d}e^{\pm j\Omega_dT_d}$, so $|z| = e^{-\sigma T_d}$ = $e^{-{{sg}}/{{fs}}}$ = {{exp(-sg/fs)||4}}.
$\angle z = \Omega_dT_d$ = 2π × {{fd|Hz}} / {{fs|Hz}} = {{Wd/fs|rad}}: the linear frequency map $\omega = \Omega T_d$.

steps.prompt: Impulse invariance turns $H_c(s) = \frac{\Omega_c}{s + \Omega_c}$ into $H(z) = \frac{\Omega_cT_d}{1 - e^{-\Omega_cT_d}z^{-1}}$. With $\Omega_cT_d$ = {{x}}, what is the DC gain $H(e^{j0})$? (The analog DC gain is 1.)
steps.explanation: At $z = 1$: $H = \frac{ {{x}} }{1 - e^{-{{x}}}}$ = {{x}} / {{1-exp(-x)||4}} = {{x/(1-exp(-x))||4}}. Two effects add up. **Aliasing**: $|H_c|$ falls only as $1/\Omega$, so the shifted copies of the spectrum add {{x/2*cosh(x/2)/sinh(x/2) - 1||2}} at DC (about $(\Omega_cT_d)^2/12$). **The jump of $h_c(t)$ at $t = 0$**: $h[0] = \Omega_cT_d$ uses the full value $h_c(0^+)$ instead of the mid-point of the jump, which adds $\Omega_cT_d/2$ = {{x/2}}. Both shrink as $\Omega_cT_d \to 0$ (sampling much faster than the cutoff), the jump term more slowly.

steps.prompt: Impulse invariance is a good method for turning an analog high-pass filter into a digital one.
steps.explanation: A high-pass response does not fall off at high frequencies, so the shifted copies in $H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_k H_c(j(\omega + 2\pi k)/T_d)$ overlap completely: severe aliasing. Impulse invariance is only suitable for band-limited (low-pass, band-pass) responses; use the bilinear transform for high-pass and band-stop filters.

steps.title: The bilinear transform
steps.body: Substituting the expression below for $s$ maps the entire $j\Omega$ axis onto the unit circle once, so there is no aliasing, and the left half plane inside it. Frequencies are warped: $\Omega = \infty$ lands at $\omega = \pi$. Drag the digital frequency to see the warping.

steps.prompt: An analog filter feature at {{f|Hz}} is mapped with the bilinear transform with $T_d = 1/f_s$, $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} (no prewarping).

ask.prompt: At which digital frequency $\omega$ does it land, in rad/sample?
ask.explanation: $\Omega T_d/2 = \pi f/f_s$ = {{pi*r||4}}, so $\omega = 2\arctan$({{pi*r||4}}) = {{w|rad}} (the linear map would give $2\pi f/f_s$ = {{2*pi*r|rad}}).

ask.prompt: Which frequency in Hz is that in the digital filter?
ask.explanation: $\omega = 2\arctan(\pi f/f_s)$ = {{w|rad}}, i.e. $\frac{\omega}{2\pi}f_s$ = {{w/(2*pi)*fs|Hz}} instead of {{f|Hz}}: the warping compresses high frequencies towards $f_s/2$.

steps.prompt: A digital low-pass at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} needs its band edge at {{fp|Hz}}. Using the bilinear transform with $T_d = 1/f_s$, at which analog frequency $\Omega_p$ must the prototype have its edge?
steps.explanation: $\omega_p = 2\pi f_p/f_s$ = {{2*pi*fp/fs|rad}}. Prewarp: $\Omega_p = \frac{2}{T_d}\tan(\omega_p/2)$ = 2 × {{fs|Hz}} × tan({{pi*fp/fs||4}}) = {{2*fs*tan(pi*fp/fs)|rad/s|4}}, a bit above $2\pi f_p$ = {{2*pi*fp|rad/s|4}}: the warping matters most close to $f_s/2$.

steps.prompt: Match each statement to the mapping or step it describes.
pairs: no aliasing, but a warped frequency axis
makes the band edges land exactly
steps.explanation: Impulse invariance keeps $\omega = \Omega T_d$ but folds the analog response. The bilinear transform squeezes the infinite $j\Omega$ axis onto the circle, so nothing folds but frequencies shift; prewarping the critical frequencies with $\Omega = (2/T_d)\tan(\omega/2)$ compensates exactly at those points. Because $T_d$ appears in both the prewarping and the transform, it drops out.

steps.prompt: A first-order low-pass $H_c(s) = \frac{\Omega_c}{s + \Omega_c}$ is mapped with the prewarped bilinear transform so that the digital −3 dB frequency is {{fc|Hz}} at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. The result is $H(z) = b_0\frac{1 + z^{-1}}{1 - pz^{-1}}$.

ask.explanation: Take $T_d = 2$ so that $s = \frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}$ and $\Omega_c = \tan(\omega_c/2) = \tan(\pi f_c/f_s)$ = {{t||4}}. Substituting gives $p = \frac{1 - \tan(\omega_c/2)}{1 + \tan(\omega_c/2)}$ = {{p||4}}.

$b_0 = \frac{\tan(\omega_c/2)}{1 + \tan(\omega_c/2)} = \frac{1 - p}{2}$ = {{(1-p)/2||4}}, with $p$ = {{p||4}}. Check: at DC $H = 2b_0/(1 - p) = 1$, and the zero at $z = -1$ is where $s = \infty$ lands.

steps.prompt: A digital Butterworth low-pass is designed with the bilinear transform: at most {{Ap}} dB loss up to $\omega_p = {{wp}}\pi$, at least {{As}} dB from $\omega_s = {{wp+dw}}\pi$. Find the minimum order.

Same kind of specifications, but now with impulse invariance (linear map $\omega = \Omega T_d$, ignoring aliasing): at most {{Ap}} dB loss up to $\omega_p = {{wp}}\pi$, at least {{As}} dB from $\omega_s = {{wp+dw}}\pi$. Find the minimum Butterworth order.
steps.explanation: With a linear map $\Omega_s/\Omega_p = \omega_s/\omega_p$ = {{wp+dw}} / {{wp}} = {{(wp+dw)/wp||4}}. $N \ge$ log₁₀({{(10^(As/10)-1)/(10^(Ap/10)-1)||4}}) / (2 log₁₀ {{(wp+dw)/wp||4}}) = {{N0||4}}, so $N$ = {{ceil(N0)}}. The bilinear transform's warping stretches the stop band away from the pass band, which is why it usually needs a lower order (and it avoids aliasing).

steps.prompt: The curve is the bilinear frequency map. A digital filter needs a band edge at $\omega = {{wt}}\pi$. Set the prewarped analog frequency $\Omega T_d$ that lands there.
steps.explanation: $\Omega T_d = 2\tan(\omega/2)$ = 2 tan({{wt/2}}π) = {{2*tan(pi*wt/2)||3}}. Close to $\omega = \pi$ the curve flattens: large analog frequencies are squeezed into a small digital range.

steps.prompt: An order-$N$ analog Butterworth low-pass is mapped with the bilinear transform. Where are the zeros of the digital filter?
steps.explanation: The analog filter has $N$ zeros at $s = \infty$ (its magnitude falls as $1/\Omega^N$). The bilinear transform maps $s = \infty$ to $z = -1$ ($\omega = \pi$): $H(z)$ gets the numerator $(1 + z^{-1})^N$. That is why bilinear low-pass filters have a true null at the Nyquist frequency.

steps.prompt: An analog Chebyshev I low-pass has {{Ap}} dB ripple up to $\Omega_p$ and must attenuate {{As}} dB at $\Omega_s$ = {{r}}$\,\Omega_p$. Find its minimum order. ($\cosh^{-1}x = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2 - 1})$.)
With prewarping, the bilinear transform reproduces the analog magnitude response at every digital frequency $\omega = \Omega T_d$.
steps.explanation: Prewarping only makes the chosen critical frequencies (the band edges) land exactly where they should. Everywhere else the response is the analog one seen through the warped axis $\Omega = (2/T_d)\tan(\omega/2)$. For piecewise-constant specifications that is harmless; it does distort, for example, a differentiator's linear magnitude.

steps.prompt: Design a digital Butterworth low-pass at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} with the bilinear transform ($T_d = 1/f_s$): at most 1 dB loss up to {{fp|Hz}}, at least {{As}} dB from {{fst|Hz}}. Match the pass-band edge exactly.

ask.prompt: At which frequency in Hz is the digital filter 3 dB down?
ask.explanation: $\Omega_c$ = {{Oc|rad/s}} maps back to $\omega_c = 2\arctan(\Omega_cT_d/2)$ = {{2*atan(Oc/(2*fs))|rad}}, i.e. $f = \frac{f_s}{\pi}\arctan\frac{\Omega_c}{2f_s}$ = {{fs/pi*atan(Oc/(2*fs))|Hz}}: above {{fp|Hz}}, since the loss there is only 1 dB.

steps.prompt: A second-order Butterworth $H_c(s) = \frac{\Omega_c^2}{s^2 + \sqrt{2}\Omega_cs + \Omega_c^2}$ is mapped with the prewarped bilinear transform to a digital cutoff $f_c$ = {{r}}$f_s$, i.e. $\omega_c = 2\pi f_c/f_s$. The result is $H(z) = b_0\frac{1 + 2z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{1 - a_1z^{-1} - a_2z^{-2}}$ (O&S sign convention). With $t = \tan(\omega_c/2)$: $b_0 = t^2/D$, $a_1 = 2(1 - t^2)/D$, $a_2 = -(1 - \sqrt{2}t + t^2)/D$ and $D = 1 + \sqrt{2}t + t^2$.

An order-{{N}} analog Butterworth low-pass with $\Omega_c = \pi/(T_d \cdot {{k}})$ is converted by impulse invariance. Aliasing is roughly the analog response at the folding frequency $\Omega = \pi/T_d$. How many dB down is the analog response there?
steps.explanation: At $\Omega = \pi/T_d$ = {{k}}$\,\Omega_c$: $10\log_{10}(1 + {{k}}^{2 \cdot {{N}}})$ = {{10*log10(1 + k^(2*N))|dB}}. Everything the analog filter passes above the folding frequency reappears below it; a higher order or a lower cutoff (relative to $1/T_d$) keeps the aliasing small.

steps.prompt: Which requirement most clearly calls for an FIR rather than an IIR filter?
options: The lowest order for a sharp magnitude cutoff
Copying the response of an existing analog filter
The shortest possible delay through the filter
steps.explanation: Only (anti)symmetric FIR filters have exactly linear phase; a stable causal IIR filter cannot. The other three favour IIR: elliptic filters reach sharp cutoffs with very low order, analog prototypes map directly to IIR filters, and a low-order IIR filter has far less delay than a long linear-phase FIR filter (whose delay is $M/2$ samples).

steps.require: min(min(Nb - floor(Nb), ceil(Nb) - Nb), min(Nc - floor(Nc), ceil(Nc) - Nc)) - 0.04
steps.prompt: Digital specs: 1 dB ripple up to $\omega_p = {{wp}}\pi$, {{As}} dB from $\omega_s = {{wp+dw}}\pi$, bilinear transform. How much lower is the Chebyshev I order than the Butterworth order?
steps.explanation: Prewarped ratio $\tan(\omega_s/2)/\tan(\omega_p/2)$ = {{rr||4}}, and $\sqrt{(10^{A_s/10} - 1)/(10^{0.1} - 1)}$ = {{sqrt(Dd)||4}}. Butterworth: log₁₀({{Dd||4}}) / (2 log₁₀ {{rr||4}}) = {{Nb||4}} → {{ceil(Nb)}}. Chebyshev: $\cosh^{-1}$({{sqrt(Dd)||4}}) / $\cosh^{-1}$({{rr||4}}) = {{Nc||4}} → {{ceil(Nc)}}. Difference: {{ceil(Nb) - ceil(Nc)}}.

steps.prompt: The bilinear transform maps every stable, causal analog filter to a stable, causal digital filter, whatever $T_d > 0$ is used.
steps.explanation: Solve the substitution for $z$: $z = \frac{1 + sT_d/2}{1 - sT_d/2}$. For $\mathrm{Re}\,s < 0$ the numerator is closer to the origin than the denominator, so $|z| < 1$: every left-half-plane pole lands inside the unit circle, for any positive $T_d$.
